problem.statement: WPF developers can't identify what's retaining memory after switching between views/controls, because standard cleanup steps (nulling data sources, forcing GC) don't reveal or fix leaks caused by hidden references (event handlers, static refs, visual tree retention) inside third-party or custom controls.

persona.primary: WPF/.NET developer maintaining a desktop app with custom/third-party UI controls

context.situation: A developer building a multi-view WPF app (matrix grid plus canvas graph) sees rendering slow down and memory climb after switching views, and basic cleanup (nulling ItemsSource, GC.Collect) does not fix it.

current_workarounds: Setting the control's ItemsSource to null on view-switch/visibility toggle
Manually forcing GC.Collect() after hiding the view
existing_substitutes: DataGrid2DLibrary (third-party WPF control involved in the leak, not a leak-diagnosis tool)

possible_wedges.offer: Standalone WPF memory-leak auditor that attaches to a running app and flags what's retaining objects after a view/control switch (event handlers, static refs, dangling bindings).
Static analysis CLI that scans WPF XAML/code-behind for known leak-prone patterns (unremoved event subscriptions, ItemsSource bindings not cleared, VisualTree retention) as part of CI/dev workflow.
Visual Studio extension that highlights leak-prone binding/event-handler patterns inline while editing XAML/code-behind.

risks: Single evidence item (one forum post) — no confirmation this is a widespread, recurring pattern rather than a one-off bug.
Zero commercial-intent signal and low urgency/commitment scores in the evidence; the poster wants free troubleshooting help, not a tool to buy.
The specific leak is tied to one obscure third-party control (DataGrid2DLibrary); unclear how well it generalizes to other WPF/audit-tooling contexts.
No mention of budget, team size, or willingness to pay anywhere in the evidence.

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: WPF developers hunting UI-switch memory leaks in third-party-control-heavy apps would use a free leak-pattern checklist/analyzer instead of manual GC.Collect() guesswork.
cheapest_experiment.input: Post a 'WPF memory leak checklist' (event handler leaks, static refs, uncleared bindings) with a free code-snippet review offer on WPF/StackOverflow-adjacent forums and relevant threads.
cheapest_experiment.output: Number of developers who submit a XAML/code-behind snippet or email for review.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: Developer pastes their code or gives their email for a free leak review.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: 10+ snippet/email submissions within 2 weeks across 3-5 forum posts.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Fewer than 3 submissions after 2 weeks despite posts getting views/replies.
